Maladaptive Strategies.value: repeatedly blame myself for what happened

Threat.value: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place

issues.item: Rumination: Self-Blame: repeatedly blame myself for what happened
issues.explanation: The self-blame item is not clinically supported elsewhere in the profile. There are no Negative Appraisal or Memory items indicating guilt, responsibility, shame, or a trauma narrative that would make repeated self-blame coherent. With this formulation, the only strong cycle is Threat ↔ Maladaptive Strategies, so maladaptive strategies should plausibly function to manage current danger/safety concerns. Drug use and avoiding thinking fit that threat-management loop, but repeated self-blame instead implies an unrepresented negative-appraisal process and sits weakly with the rest of the selected items.

vignette: The day the officers pulled him over on Elmridge Drive, Duy Tran was only trying to make it home to his wife before dinner. He had pulled into the narrow cul-de-sac behind his own house, engine idling, hands resting at ten and two on the steering wheel. When the patrol car's lights cut through the windshield, he had immediately rolled down his window and placed both palms flat on the dash. But the officers approached fast, boots heavy against the pavement, shouting commands that overlapped until his ears rang. When he stammered an explanation, one of them yanked the door open, wrenched his arms behind his back, and drove his shoulder into the curb. The cold asphalt pressed against his face, the smell of exhaust and wet concrete filling his lungs, while the weight of a knee against his lower back made every breath a sharp negotiation. What frightened him most was how quickly control had vanished; one moment he was a homeowner, the next he was pinned and powerless. He had come to believe that if he had simply stayed in his truck, or moved his hands faster, or never turned onto that street, he would have walked away unharmed. That belief settled in his chest like a stone, and it never left. Over the following weeks, Duy found himself unable to sit anywhere that didn't offer a physical barrier. In his own apartment, he began positioning his workbench and folding table so his back rested flush against the drywall, his eyes scanning the doorway every few minutes. He told himself it was just common sense, a way to keep the space under control, but his shoulders stayed knotted even when his wife left the lights on and locked the deadbolt. When the permit for a client's deck renovation stalled at the county office, he packed his tool belt and drove to the office three separate times before his lunch break, certain that a mistake meant the job was forfeited, or worse, that he would be arrested again for trespassing. Time stretched until it felt like a snare; every missed call or delayed reply convinced him that disaster was already underway. He had also started taking pills and cannabis, sitting quietly in the kitchen while he waited for his mind to go quiet. At night, he would sit on the edge of the bed and run the officers' voices backward and forward, dissecting every second until he was certain he had misread the situation, that his posture or his tone had given them reason to escalate. In the workshop, he began sanding boards until his palms blistered, forcing his attention onto the grain and the grit to keep the memory at a distance. These routines required constant focus, and he stopped accepting custom orders that required client meetings, preferring to stick to deliveries and warehouse builds where the interactions were short and scripted. His wife noticed how he flinched at the sound of sirens, how he left the television on low volume so any sudden noise wouldn't startle him, and how his own body no longer recognized safety. It was the sleeplessness that finally pushed him through the door of the community clinic. He had spent months waking at 2 a.m. with his heart hammering, convinced that if he closed his eyes, the patrol car would return. He came to the therapist's office hoping to learn how to quiet the constant readiness in his muscles, hoping to find a way to sit in a chair without checking the exits, and hoping someone could tell him he had not deserved to be pinned against the curb.
